title.en: Lesson 1. Naming the Key: The Noun-Modifying Form

blocks.md:
Remember **비가 온 것 같아요 / 오는 것 같아요 / 올 것 같아요** back in Stage 5?

We promised that the secret behind those three different verb shapes would be revealed here in Stage 6. **Here is the secret you have been waiting for!**

In English, when you want an action to describe a noun, you put words behind it: *“the book [that I bought]”* or *“the music [that I listen to]”*.

In Korean, verbs do something much more direct and elegant: they transform their ending and sit **directly in front of the noun**, acting like a descriptive modifier!

This form is called the **Noun-Modifying Form** (in Korean grammar: **관형형 / Gwanhyeong-hyeong**).

**Why is this called the Master Key?**

Because once a verb or adjective puts on this modifying shape, it can describe **any noun that follows it**, and as you will discover in the very next lesson, this single key is the hidden foundation underneath almost every major pattern you’ve learned so far!

head: Tense (시제)
Modifier Attached to Verb
Verb: 가다 (to go)
Verb: 먹다 (to eat)
Example Phrase
rows: 자주 **가는** 카페 (cafe I often go to)
내일 **갈** 카페 (cafe I will go to)

blocks.md:
**What about Adjectives (형용사)?**

Adjectives already describe an existing state or quality, so their **present** state naturally takes **-(으)ㄴ** (exactly as you already know from everyday phrases!):

- **좋다** (good) → **좋은** 날씨 (good weather)
- **작다** (small) → **작은** 가방 (a small bag)
- **예쁘다** (pretty) → **예쁜** 옷 (pretty clothes)
- **바쁘다** (busy) → **바쁜** 사람 (a busy person)
- **맵다** (spicy, ㅂ irreg) → **매운** 음식 (spicy food)

items.tip: The food I ate yesterday (Past: 먹다 + -은)
The song I am listening to right now (Present: 듣다 + -는)
The friend I will meet tomorrow (Future: 만나다 + -ㄹ)

blocks.q: Which phrase means "the coffee I drank yesterday" from 마시다 (to drink)?
blocks.why: For a past action modifying a noun, attach -(으)ㄴ: 마시- + -ㄴ = 마신 커피. (마시는 is present, 마실 is future, and 마셨 cannot directly modify a noun).

blocks.q: You look at your screen right now. How do you describe "the video I am watching right now" from 보다?
blocks.why: An ongoing present action modifying a noun takes -는: 보- + -는 = 지금 보는 영상. (본 is past "watched", 볼 is future "will watch").

blocks.meaning: The movie I watched with my friend yesterday was really fun.
blocks.why: A completed past action modifying a noun takes -(으)ㄴ: 보- + -ㄴ = 본 영화.

title.ko: 2강. 이게 다 같은 조각이었다: 8개 문법의 정체
title.en: Lesson 2. The Grand Reveal: It Was the Same Piece All Along

blocks.md:
Take a deep breath and look back at your journey from Stage 2 through Stage 5. You learned so many essential Korean expressions:

- **-(으)ㄹ 거예요** *(Future: I will do)*
- **-(으)ㄹ 때** *(Time: When I do)*
- **-(으)ㄹ 수 있다** *(Ability: I can do)*
- **-(으)ㄹ까요** *(Question / Suggestion: Shall we?)*
- **-(으)ㄹ게요** *(Promise / Intention: I will)*
- **-(으)ㄴ 후에** *(Sequence: After doing)*
- **-(으)ㄴ 적이 있다** *(Experience: I have done)*
- **-는 것 같다** *(Conjecture: It seems like)*

Did it feel like Korean was an endless sea of separate, complicated endings to memorize? **Prepare to see the entire language in a completely new light.**

**You did NOT memorize 8 different grammar rules.**

Every single one of those expressions is just the **Noun-Modifying Form** snapping directly onto a noun!

- `때` is literally a noun meaning **“time / moment”**.
- `수` is a noun meaning **“way / ability / means”**.
- `후(後)` is a noun meaning **“after / following”**.
- `적` is a noun meaning **“past instance / occasion”**.
- `것` is a noun meaning **“thing / fact / appearance”** (and `거예요` is just `것이에요` spoken quickly!).

head: Grammar Pattern
Modifier Piece
Noun / Ending Behind It
What It Literally Means
rows: “It is a thing that will happen”

blocks.md:
Look at that table again. **Everything connects!**

- When you said *“갈 거예요”*, you were literally saying **[to go + thing + is]**.
- When you said *“먹을 때”*, you were saying **[to eat + time]**.
- When you said *“한국에 간 적이 있어요”*, you were saying **[to Korea + gone + occasion + exists]**.

Korean isn’t a chaotic web of random endings. It is a breathtakingly logical set of **LEGO blocks** built on the noun-modifying system!

items.ch: 간 적이 있어요 = 간 (modifier) + 적 (occasion) + 이 있어요
오는 것 같아요 = 오는 (modifier) + 것 (appearance) + 같아요

blocks.q: In the sentence "한국에 간 적이 있어요" (I have been to Korea), what is "간"?
options: Past modifier of 가다 (가- + -ㄴ) modifying the noun 적
Present modifier of 가다 modifying the verb 있어요
blocks.why: 간 is the past modifier of 가다 (가- + -ㄴ) modifying the noun 적 (past occasion): "a past occasion of having gone exists".

blocks.q: What noun is literally hiding inside the future expression "갈 거예요" (I will go)?
options: 것 (thing / fact: 갈 것이에요 → 갈 거예요)
blocks.why: 거예요 is a spoken contraction of 것 (thing/fact) + 이에요 (is). 갈 거예요 literally means "it is a thing to go".

blocks.q: Why does "밥을 먹은 후에" mean "AFTER eating a meal"?
options: Because past modifier -(으)ㄴ attaches to 먹다 before 후 (after)
Because -은 후에 is an irregular future marker
Because 후 is a verb meaning "to eat quickly"
blocks.why: 먹은 is the past modifier of 먹다 (completed action) modifying 후 (after): "at the time after having eaten".

blocks.meaning: After class ends, shall we eat lunch together?
blocks.why: Past modifier -(으)ㄴ attaches to 끝나다 before 후에: 끝난 후에.

blocks.q: Put in order: "I have the ability to read Korean."

blocks.wrong: 시간이 있는 때 같이 커피 마셔요.
answers: 시간이 있을 때 같이 커피 마셔요.
시간이 있을 때 같이 커피 마셔요
blocks.hint: The modifier used with 때 (when) is -(으)ㄹ: 있다 → 있을 때
blocks.why: The time pattern for "~할 때" uses the prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ: 시간이 있을 때.

blocks.q: It seems to be raining right now.
blocks.hint: 지금, 비가 오다 → 오는 것 같아요

blocks.say: 수업이 끝난 후에 같이 점심 먹을까요?

title.en: Lesson 3. Creating Your Own: Modifying Any Noun Freely

blocks.md:
Up until today, you only saw noun modifiers trapped inside fixed formulas: *거예요, 때, 수 있다, 것 같다, 후에*.

**Now you are completely free.**

You know how to turn any verb into a past **-(으)ㄴ**, present **-는**, or future **-(으)ㄹ** modifier. That means **you can place them in front of ANY noun in the entire Korean language!**

Look at how you can build real-world relative clauses:

- **과거 (Past)**: *“제가 어제 **산** 책”* *(The book I bought yesterday)*
- **현재 (Present)**: *“지금 **먹는** 음식”* *(The food I am eating right now)*
- **미래 (Future)**: *“내일 **갈** 곳”* *(The place I will go tomorrow)*

**Feel the leap in your fluency!**

Before today, to express two related thoughts, you had to say two choppy sentences:
*“어제 책을 샀어요. 그 책이 재미있어요.”* *(I bought a book yesterday. That book is fun.)*

Now, you can combine them into a single, elegant sentence:
*“**어제 산 책이** 재미있어요!”* *(The book I bought yesterday is fun!)*

This is the single biggest turning point from survival-phrase Korean into true conversational fluency.

blocks.q: How do you say "The movie I watched yesterday was interesting"?
blocks.why: Modifying a noun with a completed past action (어제) takes -(으)ㄴ: 보- + -ㄴ = 본 영화. (보는 is present, 볼 is future, and 봤 cannot directly modify a noun).

blocks.q: You see a friend listening to music with headphones. How do you ask: "What is the song you are listening to right now?"
blocks.why: An ongoing present action modifying a noun takes -는: 듣- + -는 = 듣는 노래. (들은 is past, 들을 is future).

blocks.q: How do you say "I have a place I will go tomorrow"?
blocks.why: A future destination modifying 곳 (place) takes -(으)ㄹ: 가- + -ㄹ = 갈 곳. (가는 is present, 간 is past).

blocks.meaning: The food that I like the most is tteokbokki.
blocks.why: General present preference modifying 음식 takes -는: 좋아하- + -는 = 좋아하는 음식.

blocks.q: Put in order: "This is the coffee I drink every morning."
Build the phrase: "the book I bought yesterday"
blocks.why: Past modifier for 사다 is 산 (사- + -ㄴ) modifying 책: 어제 산 책.

blocks.q: Build the sentence: "What is the place we will go tomorrow?"
blocks.why: Future modifier for 가다 is 갈 (가- + -ㄹ) modifying 곳: 내일 갈 곳이 어디예요?

blocks.wrong: 지금 내가 읽은 책이 정말 재미있어요.
answers: 지금 내가 읽는 책이 정말 재미있어요.
지금 내가 읽는 책이 정말 재미있어요
blocks.hint: For an action happening right now (지금), use present modifier -는: 읽는 책
blocks.why: Present action modifying a noun takes -는: 지금 내가 읽는 책이 정말 재미있어요.

blocks.hint: For someone you met yesterday (어제), use past modifier -(으)ㄴ: 만난 사람
blocks.why: Past action modifying a noun uses -(으)ㄴ: 어제 만난 사람이 제 친구예요.

blocks.q: The coffee I drank yesterday was really delicious.
blocks.hint: 어제, 마시다 → 마신 커피, 정말 맛있었어요
blocks.why: Past modifier is 마신: 어제 마신 커피가 정말 맛있었어요.

blocks.q: What is the song you are listening to right now?
blocks.why: Present modifier is 듣는: 지금 듣는 노래가 뭐예요?

blocks.say: 제가 어제 산 책이 정말 재미있어요.

title.en: Lesson 4. Connecting Time: Past, Present & Future Modifiers

blocks.h: Putting Past, Present & Future Modifiers Together
blocks.md:
Now you have the master key to describing nouns across all three timeframes!

- **과거 (Past)**: **-(으)ㄴ + 명사** *(어제 만난 친구 = friend I met yesterday)*
- **현재 (Present)**: **-는 + 명사** *(지금 듣는 노래 = song I am listening to now)*
- **미래 (Future / Plan)**: **-(으)ㄹ + 명사** *(내일 먹을 점심 = lunch I will eat tomorrow)*

In daily life, Koreans constantly use these modifiers with generic nouns like **것/거** *(thing)*, **사람** *(person)*, **곳** *(place)*, and **때** *(time)*:
- **제가 좋아하는 것** *(things I like)*
- **내일 갈 곳** *(places to go tomorrow)*
- **어제 산 거** *(things I bought yesterday)*

blocks.why: For a future plan or prospective action (내일), attach -(으)ㄹ to the stem: 가- + -ㄹ = 갈 곳.

blocks.q: Which sentence talks about the coffee someone drank earlier?
blocks.why: For past completed action earlier (아까), use the past modifier -(으)ㄴ: 마신 커피.
